newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader assumes new powers after poll win.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader assumes new powers after poll win.

text.p: Opponents of President Alexander Lukashenko face a crucial test on Tuesday when parliament reassembles following his crushing victory in a weekend referendum to extend his powers.
The president met deputies loyal to him on Monday at a building opposite his residence but ignored his main foe, speaker Semyon Sharetsky, and other parliamentary leaders.
Opposition deputies were planning to hold their own session to try to pass a resolution to declare the polls invalid.
"It's a farce," Sharetsky said. "Belarus is heading for a real dictatorship."
Lukashenko was in a conciliatory mood as he claimed victory on Monday, saying he was sure he would not have to hold new parliamentary elections and "peace and harmony" would be found.
The new constitution allows him to dissolve parliament and call elections if the chamber fails to approve the formation of a 64-seat upper house and 110 deputies in the lower house.
The United States on Monday said Lukashenko's victory was "deprived of legitimacy."

"We're quite disappointed that in Belarus yesterday the government went ahead with this referendum that has been labeled by the (Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe) and other international organisations as deprived of legitimacy," said State Department spokesman Glyn Davies.
The constitutional court had also been scheduled to sit on Tuesday to consider a request by parliament to remove the president from office for ignoring the old constitution.

But press spokesman Igor Maskalyov on Monday said the court would probably not meet. He was speaking after Lukashenko said the 11 judges, who have overruled a string of his decrees, would have to toe the line in future to keep their jobs.
"I do not exclude many members of the court will be part of the new one in the interests of continuity -- if they give up their political bias," he said.

Lukashenko also seemed sure the judges would not rule against him, a move which would transfer power to Sharetsky pending a parliament vote. Asked what he would do if they did, he said: "You think they will?"
The referendum result had been seen as a foregone conclusion, especially since state television and radio ran a string of items each day showing how to vote for Lukashenko and against parliament.

Viktor Gonchar, the country's top electoral official appointed by parliament but sacked by Lukashenko after he declared the poll invalid in advance, said the turnout of more than 84 percent was so high it must have been faked.
But Lukashenko dismissed accusations that the vote was based on massive fraud and the outcome decreed in advance.
Lukashenko easily won all four questions set by him while parliament's proposals were trounced -- a fact that deputies also said indicated an unfair vote.

"It will be very hard for my opponents to insist there were violations, that the referendum was illegal. The overwhelming majorities won by all the president's questions speak for themselves," Lukashenko told a news conference.
The constitution will now give him the right to name half the commission which monitors and approves voting and is currently run by Lidiya Yermoshina, appointed by Lukashenko.
There was also no mention by the central electoral commission, state television, or Lukashenko of the results of by-elections to 51 vacant seats in parliament.

Since winning the presidency by a landslide in July 1994, Lukashenko has become increasingly authoritarian, and he will now have powers that a Council of Europe analysis recently said "could not be stronger".
Parliament's draft constitution, which would have abolished the presidency and strengthened parliament, won the backing of just 7.9 percent of the electorate.
The electorate also voted overwhelmingly to keep the death penalty, let Lukashenko continue appointing local leaders and to keep a ban on the free sale and purchase of land.
"This election was decided before it began," the head of the International Helsinki Federation in Vienna, Aaron Rhodes, said by telephone.
